lede: The question of where agent memory should live has a boring answer: in files, in a folder, in the repository, under version control. The interesting questions start afterwards. Who can see what the system currently believes? Which page is the entry point when there are two hundred? Which instruction is still true? In an agent-first team those questions decide what the next run does, and answering them is maintenance work of the same kind as maintaining code. This article describes how one delivery system keeps its memory visible, organised and current, and where that discipline still fails.

p: Volume against legibility. Agents write far more than humans can read; living documents, reports, decision records and sidecars accumulate by the hundred. A memory nobody can survey is a memory nobody can correct.

Locality against discoverability. Files are cheapest to maintain next to the thing they describe, but an agent reasoning about a topic needs one place to start. Without a designated entry point every run re-derives the state of the world, and derivations diverge.

Stability against currency. A recorded decision is valuable because it does not change; an operational instruction is valuable only while it is true. Both look the same in a folder. Treating them alike either freezes guidance that should expire or rewrites history that should stand.

Machine writing against human curation. Pipeline steps can append, link and grade tirelessly; only a human can say which of three open dossiers is the one that matters now. If curation is not a scheduled, visible act, the machine layer buries the human one.

New work against in-flight work. The cheapest reaction to an observation is a new card. If the observation is not reconciled against what is already open, the board fills with duplicates and the memory with contradicting plans.

Agent Studio keeps the knowledge behind its own development as living documents it calls dossiers. A dossier is a folder under docs/ with an index.html and a workbench.json descriptor; the code identifiers stay workbench while the product noun is dossier, by a recorded naming decision. The descriptor carries an id that must equal the folder name, a status, a phase, a summary, the keys of the tasks that produced it and of the tasks it relates to, and its own key in the AGT-W series. Status is one of active, decision-pending, decided, documented or archived; a second descriptor version replaces status with a lifecycle state of in-progress, review-requested, decided, documented or done. The explorer lists active, decision-pending and decided dossiers by default and moves documented and archived ones under a History toggle where they remain readable and linkable. A descriptor with a value outside those enums renders the dossier as invalid in the list, which is a feature: a broken pointer is visible rather than silently absent.

Curation is explicit. Decisions are recorded inline in the dossier, as checkboxes and free text next to the analysis that supports them, and a decision outcome either spawns feature cards or archives the dossier with a reason. One dossier, the Nordstern, is the single entry point for the target-picture complex; it holds the big arc and links into the deep-dive documents, which are kept focused and set to decided so that they live under History. The repository's root instruction file, AGENTS.md, is canonical; CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md and the Copilot instructions are one-line shims that point to it. Adding a document under docs/ requires adding one row to the start index in the same change. An opt-in pipeline step regenerates a small registry of designated topics, so that agents, in the registry's own words, read the current state of a topic instead of re-discovering it.

The work maintains the memory. A card that references a dossier must append an entry inside a marker-delimited, append-only implementation log in that dossier; a pipeline step checks the diff and fails the card if the dossier changed outside that region or if existing entries were edited or reordered. After review, another step appends the card to the relatedTasks list in the page's .meta.json sidecar and commits it with a message of the form 'chore(wiki): link AGT-NNNN to docs/...'. The sidecar is deliberately deletion-tolerant: a reference to a card that no longer exists stays as history. Agent reads per page are counted, so an operator can see which documents are actually consulted.

Currency is measured, not assumed. The wiki's landing view bands every page by the number of commits under the code roots since the page was last edited: Fresh below ten, Aging up to forty-nine, Stale from fifty; the rule is deterministic and needs no model. An operator can trigger a grading run that writes a machine grade from A to D with short feedback into the page's sidecar, together with a fingerprint of the graded source so that an unchanged page is not graded twice. A separate drift auditor writes its findings as Markdown reports into a docs/.drift folder. Decisions that are load-bearing go into a single ADR archive with monotonic numbers; a later decision supersedes an earlier one rather than deleting it.

New work is reconciled against in-flight work before it exists. The task-API skill instructs every agent to search existing tasks before creating one, and a duplicate slug is answered with a 409 conflict rather than a second card. During supervised hours the orchestrating session keeps a live improvement log in which every observation receives one of three verdicts before it may become work: covered-by, naming the open card that already owns it; operator-action, when a hand has to move and no ticket is needed; or new-candidate, which becomes a card only after a second sighting or an operator's nod. The same session keeps its own memory as an index file with one line per note and one note per durable fact, each with a reason and a how-to-apply section, and corrections are appended as dated updates rather than written over.

p: The human role shifts from writing documents to curating them: deciding what is the entry point, what is decided, what is archived, which observation is already covered. That role is small in keystrokes and large in effect, because every agent run starts from the state this curation leaves behind.

Visibility becomes a property of the tooling rather than of diligence. A list with lifecycle states, a History toggle, sidecars that name the cards behind a page and read counters per page let an operator see what the system believes without opening every file. The same surfaces make drift noticeable: a Stale band or a D grade next to a page that agents keep reading is an actionable signal.

Organisation is enforced at a few chokepoints instead of everywhere: id equals folder, one canonical instruction file, one row in the start index per new document, one entry point per topic complex. Everything else can stay local to the feature.

Currency has a cost centre. Grading runs spend tokens, drift audits spend attention, and append-only logs grow. The system keeps the deterministic signals free and the model-judged ones opt-in, which is the right default: a currency check that runs on every change becomes a gate nobody reads.

The memory layer becomes the place where the rest of the operating model is legible. The verdicts, overrides and requeue reasons that make pull-request-free delivery reviewable are memory too; if they are not kept current, the verdict stream stops meaning anything. See the companion article, Skip the Pull Request.

When the volume does not exist yet. A team with a dozen documents and one agent needs a README and a decision log, not lifecycle states, sidecars and grading runs. Add the machinery when the list stops fitting on a screen.
When the memory is not shared. Scratch notes of a single session do not need review history or a lifecycle; keep them ephemeral and promote only the facts that should affect future work.

When a narrow requirement demands another store. High-volume event streams, transactional coordination, cross-repository retrieval at scale, confidentiality or deletion obligations can justify a database, a vector index or a secrets manager. Keep the human-agent contract in files and treat the other store as derived or as a pointer target, because every second place is a place where visibility, organisation and currency can diverge.

When nobody will curate. The mechanisms above make curation visible and cheap; they do not perform it. A system that appends, links and grades without anyone deciding what is current produces a well-instrumented pile.

Descriptors that drift from their own schema. Dossiers have been written by hand with a phase outside the allowed set and appeared as invalid in the explorer until corrected; a dossier's prose has called itself accepted while its descriptor said decided, because accepted is not a state. The enum is the memory of what the states mean, and it is the first thing a hurried author forgets.

Stale pointers inside the documents that are supposed to prevent staleness. The task-API skill still links to an ADR anchor that was renumbered when a merge conflict was cleaned up; an accepted ADR names implementation paths from before a folder reorganisation; the wiki-tree contract lists four lifecycle states where the schema and the code have five. Each is small, each was found by reading, and each would have steered an agent that trusted it.

Currency by design rather than by accident. The Nordstern declares that it goes stale on schedule and defers to dated situation snapshots; sidecar references to deleted cards are kept on purpose; the drift folder holds one report so far. These are deliberate trade-offs, but they mean that 'current' has to be read off the signals rather than assumed from the presence of a page.

A naming decision that saves a rename and costs a translation forever. The product noun is dossier; the code, the file names, the routes and the keys say workbench. The decision is recorded and the reasons are sound, and every newcomer still has to learn the mapping.

Parts of the memory model that are still proposals. The orchestrator's own compact working-memory snapshot, a visible and rebuildable briefing of what it currently knows, is written up and accepted as a non-goal for hidden memory, but it is not built; what exists today is a durable event log and a read-only digest of lane counts, quota and recent verdicts. Grading is operator-triggered, not scheduled. The discipline described above is real; the automation behind it is uneven.
